utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This is Thursday, and I welcome representatives from the Prosecution, Mr. Scott and Mr. Stringer. Welcome counsel for Defence and our four accused. It seems that two are ill, Mr. Coric and Mr. Petkovic. I would ask Mr. Coric's counsel whether his client is really ill. Is he ill? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Coric, as far as we've been informed, suffers from some sort of virus. It's not a serious illness, but he feels too sick to attend these proceedings. But there's nothing seriously wrong with him, and I expect him to return to the courtroom next week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now give the floor to the registrar to obtain an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Marita Vihervuori: The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 645. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 646. List of objections to be tendered: The OTP response to be -- to the list of documents tendered by 2D through Witness Antoon van der Grinten shall be given Exhibit number IC 647. The OTP response to the list of documents tendered through Witness Antoon van der Grinten shall be given be Exhibit number IC 648. That is the response to the list of documents tendered through 3D. And next, the OTP response to the list of documents tendered by 6D through Witness Antoon van der Grinten shall be given Exhibit number IC 649. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. After the problem we had with the electrical power failure, we have a decision to give and I will read it slowly. Oral decision regarding the witness's impossibility to answer a question on grounds of "force majeure." Following an interruption in the hearing for reasons of "force majeure" on Tuesday, August 28, 2007, around 1.45 p.m., Prosecution was unable to obtain an answer from the witness after a question asked. The Trial Chamber believes that the question asked, which dealt with an alleged ultimatum dating January 1993, is of limited interest regarding Witness Vihervuori. The Trial Chamber believes that not obtaining an answer to this question is not detrimental to Prosecution. On these grounds, Chamber declares the hearing closed without having heard the answer from this witness. So this was a decision that was required in connection with the hearing that was not -- that couldn't close normally because of this power failure, the power failure that prohibited us from hearing the witness's answer and also thanking the answer. I'm sure the witness understood this was force majeure, act of God. Furthermore, the Chamber would like to add one thing for Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Praljak. Yesterday, we had the problem of the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: and we confirm also today, that when an accused asks a question, he can only do so within the ruling of May 10, 2007, paragraph 12. For this reason, the Chamber is asking Mr. Praljak to meet its counsel -- his counsel before the hearing, to meet with Mr. Kovacic, to give him all necessary instructions regarding the questions that will be asked during the cross-examination; if need be, to write down the question and hand it over to the counsel who will read it, in order to distribute the roles between the counsel which has a role to play and the accused that can also take the floor but only exceptionally. And this should help things run smoothly. Furthermore, the Chamber -- the Trial Chamber underlines that, when an accused will take the floor to ask questions, his counsel will have to tell the Trial Chamber, prior to his taking the floor, what are the reasons why the accused wants to take the floor. The Prosecution might then object - I don't know whether it will or not - and Chamber can immediately consult and allow or deny, which was what was written in the decision of May 10. We wanted to remind Mr. Praljak of these instruction. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for those instructions. My client, General Praljak, and I myself have discussed the matter, of course, already, and I have prepared short notes to put forward. I can put forward those arguments at any point in time why we consider that following the decision of the 10th of May should be given the right and opportunity to cross-examine the witness. So I'm ready to go ahead with those arguments whenever you wish to hear them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we will continue with the witness's hearing. But before this, late afternoon, yesterday, we found out that next week it would be impossible, technically, to hear the witness that was scheduled, because his government must provide an authorisation. Mr. Scott, do you confirm this? The hearing of the witness that was planned for next week is going to be postponed sine die.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honour, all of Your Honours, Mr. President, all the Judges, and all those in the courtroom. Your Honour, just out of an abundance of caution, if we could go into private session, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to going into private session at this point. I think, it's obvious, there's an open record with respect to the witness's prior occupation. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: An unconfirmed allegation and rumour has been put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has consulted and believes that we need to go into private hearing, because the Prosecution might going into topics that we don't know about. We can't know ahead of time what's going to say. I'm not in Mr. Scott's brain nor in Mr. Karnavas's brain. So please could we a have a private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the upcoming witness is concerned, the Prosecution had not completed its examination-in-chief. There was another series of questions that needed to be asked, and I think that Mr. Stringer will need something between 50 minutes and one hour to complete his examination-in-chief. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. It is my understanding that I have 50 minutes left, and I will be -- I expect to use all of those 50 minutes, but hopefully cannot ask for anything more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the cross-examination is concerned, the Trial Chamber had indicated last week that each accused would have 30 minutes. If we can't finish today, then, of course, if we have some extra time, we will continue the testimony of this witness on Monday afternoon, and we can then complete this witness's testimony by Monday if we haven't finished --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Or on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if the following situation arises, and if we cannot finish this witness's testimony today but that on Monday at a quarter past 2.00, the other witness is ready, then today's witness will have to come back at a latter stage. This is how we need to proceed. I think everybody agrees on this. So we shall now bring in the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'd like to welcome you on behalf of my colleagues. As you know, the examination-in-chief will resume today, and the cross-examination will also begin today. I, therefore, give the floor to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Good morning, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we begin, I ask the gentleman in the technical booth, we have the PowerPoint presentation loaded on the computer here, if it is possible to put on the screen so that everyone can following along with the PowerPoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And while that's being done, Witness, just to bring us up to -- up-to-date, last week, during your direct examination, you testified about a report that you'd prepared dealing with the issue of population movements within eight municipalities of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then, right at the end of that day, we were able to conclude your testimony on that report with some conclusions. So now what I'd like to do is go directly into the other two reports that you've prepared, bearing in mind that we probably need to try and complete our testimony here within the next 50 minutes or so. On the screen, and just to continue with that, we've not had any communication, so I'll just let you know that in preparing for this morning, I'm going to skip through some of the slides that we previously had intended to -- to look at and go directly to your conclusions. Now, did you prepare, Ms. Tabeau, a report related to the numbers of persons killed in East Mostar during the course of the conflict there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, in general and briefly, what were your objectives in preparing that report? Tell us what are the sources of information on which you relied, and, again, very briefly and in general, the methods used in preparing that report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of this report was to produce reliable statistics on that coast in the city of East Mostar in the period from the 9th of May, 1993 until approximately April 1994. Sources that can be used in these kind of study are infrequent. East Mostar is a very small area that is not easy statistically defined. So the choice of sources that we used had to take this into account. There was one source that actually suited the needs of this project very well. This was the hospital records of Mostar war hospital books, from Mostar war hospital books. This hospital was located in East Mostar, and all patients treated in this hospital actually were coming from East Mostar area. And this was the area where they acquired their injuries and where they killed -- they were killed. But, of course, this source covered only a small group of victims. As victims who were killed were directly and were dead immediately were not brought to the hospital, we had to use additional sources. The additional sources was the records from Mostar death registries. This is the source that is very commonly used in statistics and demography. This is the registration part of the vital events registration system in every country. In this particular case, we used the death registries from the area that was -- from the area in Mostar that was controlled by the -- by the Bosnian -- by the Bosniaks. So, because of this split of Mostar at the beginning of the conflict into two parts, the West and East Mostar, the authorities started around that time in early 1993 to keep their records separately. So we used the death registries that were reporting on the deaths of Bosniaks, of the Muslim population. So this was another source that was very useful and very good for our study. We had to be careful with the selection of records. As I said, East Mostar is a small area. So we had to make sure that records we included were relevant and were -- could be considered as deaths related to the city of East Mostar. One more source that we included are the military records of soldiers and other military personnel killed during the Bosnian war. We have in our unit three lists, military lists from three armies; the ABiH army, the VRS army, and the HVO. All together these lists cover approximately 48.000 records, and they covered the entire conflict period. We used this source as a reference source. In our sources, such as West Mostar war hospital books and Mostar death registries, the reporting of the military civilian status is not complete. It's deficient. So it was important to use the military lists in order to mark militaries in our records from the major sources. I want to stress the military records include more than just fallen soldiers. This list includes also persons or personnel who worked in the Ministry of Defence in every political entity. They also include deaths of the people working in production section providing service and goods for the army. So these sources, as a reference, it includes more than just the fallen soldiers, the combatants who died in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, and the methods, as indicated on the slide, you employed a counting approach and then combined that with some statistical estimation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Our basic approach is always counting. We try to -- to collect as many records as we can, and we try to present counts, minimum numbers of victims. But depending on -- on the situation with sources, in most cases sources are very incomplete. We try to compensate for the deficiencies and incompleteness of sources, and we combine the counting approach with some statistical estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to focus briefly on the war hospital, the war hospital books?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, these war hospital records are already in evidence in this case. They were admitted in the course of the testimony of a witness who appeared, one of the doctors who worked at the hospital, and he testified in this case last January. And with the assistance of the technical booth, I'd ask if we could, perhaps from e-court, put up Exhibit P 02786 on the screens. This is one of the hospital books that is in evidence that was testified about, and it's the smallest one, so we're able to work with it. Do we have that on the screen? We don't need translation. We can use the full screen for this. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, and just I think it's useful, Ms. Tabeau, let's focus on the third entry. First of all, is this a page from -- does this appear to be a page from the war hospital records that you relied on in making your study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is this page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is also the same war hospital book that you used in making the other study that you're going to be talking about in a few minutes which relates to the wounded people in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same source, the same books.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just focusing on the third entry there, I think it may be useful for everyone to understand how you worked. What we see here is an entry, number 4545, I believe. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the name -- well, can you tell us, moving across from left to right, what the information on this page means to you in respect of your report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the war hospital books, patients are registered as they were arriving in the hospital. Each patient received a number in the books; and, in the case we are looking at, it is the number 4545. So patients have consecutive numbers, and the books are organised according to the calendar time of their arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just jump in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, as we are counting backwards, it looks as though we're talking about entry number 4543.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I misread that. Yes, that's right. Yes. Well, there are date stamps in the hospital books. The first patient arriving at a given day also received a day stamp, which I can't see on this particular page. But I'm pretty sure if we could go down or up a little bit, then -- not on this page. Perhaps down. Next one perhaps. Well, from the date stamp, it clear when exactly the patient arrived; then we have the name of the patient reported. In this particular case, it is Senad Bacejevic, I think. I might have read it incorrectly. In the next field, it is reported that the person was a Vojnik, which is a soldier; and in the last field, there is the diagnosis. It's given in Latin. What I can see here is a familiar term, "V. explosiva," which comes from "vulnus explosiva." This is a term that was consequently used for victims of shelling. There are also some other terms in the field of diagnosis, different than "vulnus explosiva." It might be "vulnus trans-sclopetarium," or sclopetarium," which would be the term used for a person wounded by a gunshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But going back to this record we are discussing, I would also like to draw attention to the circle around the number of this patient, 4543. The circle is one of the markers that were used in the books. The circle were used for people that died, didn't survive. And in the field of diagnosis, you can read in the last line that this patient is "adit exit sletelus" [phoen], or something like that, which means that the person died.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. According to this record, then, this tells us that this individual was a soldier, that he was admitted to the hospital for some sort of explosive wound -- explosive wounding, and that he ultimately died then from his wounds.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it says. We have the name of the person. We don't have the year of birth of the person, but we know that he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, just to anticipate this issue in respect of your other report on the wounded people, let's just talk now about this. For all of these patients who are -- who are referenced in these records -- and by the way, did you review all of the war hospital records that we have on this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We reviewed all these records, one by one. The reason was that we didn't computerise the records. We received an electronic version of the records, and we wanted to make sure that there are no mistakes, no omissions, that everything is correct. So all these records have been reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, on the basis your analysis of this -- this report, then, did you not then take this information and merge it with other data that was available to you and the other sources that you've described, the death registers and the military lists?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end we did, but we also studied each source separately and we compared the sources. But in the end, we merged the sources, combined the sources. Two major sources combined were the records from the war hospital books and the records from the death registries. Each of these source have been also matched with the military lists; and through the links with the military lists, we improved the reporting of the military civilian status of the victims in our master list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So, now, if we could just return to the PowerPoint slide, because I'm going to skip ahead to one that I want to ask you about and that is this. Again, the Trial Chamber heard your explanation about this before, but I think it may bear repeating very briefly: The distinction or the difference between absolute minimum numbers and the more complete minimum numbers based on the actual counting and then the estimation method that you employed.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, minimum, absolute minimum numbers, come from the counting approach. These numbers are just obtained by looking at the master list of combined sources, and we take the victims reported in the master list and count how many are there and this is the absolute minimum. But because the sources are deficient and several information items are missing, it is important to compensate for this, and this is when the proportion-based approach comes into work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And again the proportion-based approach is the one that yields what you called a more complete absolute minimum number.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, what I want to do is cut right to the end of this part of the PowerPoint, and just go straight to the conclusions so that we're sure to cover all of those here; and then as time permits, either I or counsel for the Defence can bring you back to these individual items for more discussion. So, Ms. Tabeau, why don't you just go down these points and tell us the conclusions, the final results that you reached in course of this study of the deaths of the killed people in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The absolute minimum number of deaths obtained from the counting approach and based on the master list of combined sources is 539 deaths. Of this number, we certainly know this is a heavy underestimation. There was certainly many more deaths resulting from the siege of East Mostar. But because of the deficiencies and incompleteness of the sources, we are unable to include more deaths in the absolute minimum number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, again, the absolute minimum number being the number of -- this is the number of individuals whose names you can provide based on the sources that you've already described?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The more complete number of deaths within should be 1.023, and this is a number that tries to compensate for the incompleteness of sources. One major deficiency of the war hospital records is that a number of pages are missing in these books. In total, 465 records are reported on the missing pages, so we had to exclude this number of records from the calculation of the absolute minimum. In the death registries, the major deficiency is that a large number of records, approximately 460, have no place of death reported, even though we know that a large number of them are from Mostar. We are unable to decide whether these deaths are from exactly East Mostar or not; otherwise, these records would be consistent with the time frame of the siege. So these records had to be excluded from the absolute number as well. But taking this into account, we believe that the more complete minimum number is the 1.023 deaths that we report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further, we studied the civilian military distribution of the victims. We applied two methods to make an assessment of this distribution, and the result of both methods was similar. There is approximately 50 per cent of deaths that should be considered as deaths of civilians. Further, approximately 90 per cent, specifically speaking 87.8 per cent of deaths, were of Muslims. This is the largest group of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just jump in there and ask if you could tell the Trial Chamber, please, how you went about determining who were civilians versus militaries, and also how you went about determining ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian military status was reported in the war hospital books. The reporting was not fully complete, but it was complete enough to look at the distribution of civilians versus militaries. So this was one way that we estimated the percentage of civilian victims in our total. We just obtained a proportion of civilians and militaries from the war hospital books and applied this proportion to the master list of combined sources. That was methods one. But to make sure that our estimate is correct, that there is no error involvement, we have redone the estimation based on the improved reporting of the military civilian status. This improved reporting was obtained through the matches of the records from Mostar war hospital books and from Mostar death registries with the military lists. Every person matched with the military list was considered to be a military person. For others, we kept the reporting as available. The results of these two methods are exactly the same, almost exactly the same, very similar. This is 50/50 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me jump in. I want to make sure we understand that. You used two methods to calculate the proportion of civilian versus military deaths; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the first method was -- was based on the review of the war hospital records themselves, the document that we've looked at already.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after that, you got a proportion based on that, that review.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had to be war hospital books because it was the only source where the reporting was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the death registries, there is no information about civilian-military distribution of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you introduced additional data, that being from the military lists?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after using that second method, then, how did the results compare as between the two methods?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said several times already, the results are very similar. So the method based on improved reporting of the military-civilian status through the links with the military lists resulted in the same type of distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that distribution indicated here would be 49.5 per cent of the siege-related deaths were civilian.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. We believed that it might have been more civilians, as I know that our military lists overestimated the -- the combatants and militaries, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then in terms of ethnicity, I'm not sure, how did you determine ethnicity for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ethnicity was not originally was not reported in the sources. In the war hospital books, ethnicity was determination on the basis of studying the names of the victims; and, in this project, the ethnicity was determined by native B/C/S speakers familiar with the naming traditions in this area. So this wasn't done in my unit. It was done before I received the data for my analysis, but we didn't have to do anything. This is often done and, well, there are differences in naming tradition between the ethnic groups. And people who are from the region are able to decide based on names the ethnicity of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the death registries, we applied a different approach. We used information from the 1991 population census; namely, we studied the ethnic distribution of the same names as those reported in the death registries. We studied the ethnic distribution of these names in the population census, and we took for every person the prevailing reporting of ethnicity for a given name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was a statistical approach, an approach based on what was observed in the population census, and we just followed the results. We decided for every person that the ethnic group that most frequently had this given name is the ethnicity that should be assigned to this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I should have asked you this at the beginning: What's the time frame for this study? What is the period of time that you examined in reaching these numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is from May 1993 to approximately April -- actually, in war hospital books, it is also May 1994 that is included. It's approximately one-year period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning period, is it from the 9th of May or is it from the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it is the 9th of May. This is the first date where the records from war hospital books --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- are available, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now the next point here indicates the frequency of death seen in the records was greatest during August and September, and you indicate this is contrary to what would be expected. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, expected is what we expect in relation to a phenomenon based on the knowledge of the phenomenon we have, and here the expected seasonal mortality pattern is what we often see in mortality pattern when observed over time. It is not that people die equally, frequently throughout the whole year. In the period of summer, we observe that the level of mortality is much lower in the summer and in the fall, than in the winter and early spring. So winter months are usually the months when the levels of mortality are the highest, winter and early spring months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So finding that the greatest number of deaths here occurred during August and September is inconsistent with what one finds in a normal population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not only inconsistent; it is just opposite to what is normally seen when you look at mortality pattern over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, point of clarification. Normal population. Are we speaking about Bosnia-Herzegovina or we speaking about in general, you know, Asia, the Middle East, Africa? Is this the general wide-sweeping conclusion, or is this in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that people die more frequently in the winter than they do, say, in the spring or summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- of course, I'm speaking of Europe and the same climate zone in which Bosnia and Herzegovina is located. Well, in Europe in this climate, that is the observation of seasonality that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next item, then, you break down the cause of death. Could you explain -- well, it's obviously self-evident: Shelling deaths, gunshot deaths, and then 44.3 deaths being of violent nature but unspecified. First of all, on the shelling and gunshot, is that taken information taken directly from the causes of death, for example, that we saw with this the one on the war hospital record who died?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, causes of death were reported in both sources. In war hospital records, causes of death were reported more frequently and were available in a larger extent than in the death registries. Reporting of causes of death in the death registry is really very poor, but there are victims of shelling and gunshots reported in the death registries as well. We actually based our distribution of deaths by cause of death on the reporting, on the distribution observed in the war hospital records. The proportions of deaths from shelling, gunshots, and violent deaths of unspecified causes come from the war hospital records. These proportions were applied to the master list of combined sources, to the list of 539 deaths; and by doing this, we could present also the absolute minimum number of deaths by cause. But in percentage terms, 45.3 per cent were deaths caused by shelling, 10.4 per cent were deaths by gunshots, and 44.3 per cent were violent deaths of unspecified cause. We are unable to say whether these were victims of shelling or gunshots, but we know these were violent deaths related to the siege of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How do you know they were violent deaths?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of the patients who were brought to the war hospital because of their wounds they acquired during the siege, these were the people who died of these wounds in the war hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were other medical facilities or clinics available for the people in East Mostar during this time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we speak of in-patient facilities like the -- like hospitals, then the war hospital is the only facility of this kind. But I am aware that there were a number of outpatient facilities in this area. These were small places that, however, could be contacted by the patients and aid would be provided. I think there were at least four first-aid clinics, if we can call them clinics, and some other, like four perhaps more, out-patient clinics in which aid could be provided. Very basic aid though, I must stress. I don't think these out-patient clinics had the equipment that would be useful for surgeries or more complex aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the gravely ill patients, then, were the ones who would be reflected in the war hospital records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you include records of these other clinics, out-patient clinics, in either this study or in your study of the wounded people in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have these records, so it is that we are unable to say how many patients were treated in the out-patient clinics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Moving back to the slide. You've calculated that 18.7 per cent of the people who died were females. What is that based on?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sex is reported in every source. It is a very complete reporting. So in the master list in every record, almost every record the sex is available, so that's the proportion. 18.7 per cent of deaths were women.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then moving to the next item, over a fifth of the dead people were younger than 19 or over 64. How did you arrive at those figures?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is also that, for most victims, year of birth is available or a complete date of birth; so having these two, year of death and year of birth, it was possible to obtain the age of victims. For Many victims, age was reported as well. So this is another item that is available relatively easily from the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to -- just to amplify that a bit. Yes. This is a slide that breaks that last point down a little bit on the bottom part. In terms of children and elderly, how do the numbers break down?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these percentages that we just discussed can be seen here as 58 children and youth below the age of 19 years. Eleven of them were girls. And when it comes to the elderly, there were 63 people at page 65 or more years, and 24 of them were women.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So then it's the combination of these two percentages that give the 22.5 per cent figure that we saw on the next slide?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. And then the final point, again, I think it's been made, why are these such conservative minimum numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these numbers are so conservative because sources that were used were incomplete and deficient in several ways. So the sources didn't allow us to accept more records to be included in the absolute minimum numbers. At the same time, we are very convinced that absolute minimum numbers are far too low, and the more complete minimum number is approximately 1.023 deaths. This number is in line with other estimates made by other people, which I did not discuss in this report. So I probably won't go into it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then, in the time that's left to us, Ms. Tabeau, we will move then to the final report that you prepared based upon what appear to be the same source of data; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same source and it's the major source, and it was the only source used for the estimation of the wounded persons, for obtaining statistics on the wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that source being, again, being the hospital records --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostar war hospital books.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- such as the one we looked at earlier. All right. Now, before we get into these numbers, the approach that you employed in making this report, is it an approach that you've used in making other reports or other testimonies here at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the source as such is hospital records. It's not used for the first time in my work. I also work with these records when I was making my reports on the siege of Sarajevo, and this is a very useful source and usually very reliable. Well, I have good experience with these kind of records also from the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The approach, of course, counting and estimations, statistical estimation, it's exactly same as what we applied in the case of killed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so what we'll see is that estimation, then, is applied to determine the breakdown types of wounding as between the -- the wounded individuals who you've counted.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please. When you're talking about the wounded, what kind of wounds are you talking about, military wounds or traffic accidents that would result in wounds? So what kind of wounds are involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the case of war hospital records, the wounds that we are talking about are wounds acquired from shelling or gunshots. That is the type of wounds that are reported in the diagnosis field available from these records. There are no wounds related to traffic accidents or reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could go back to Exhibit P 02786 and look at that again now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we could examine some of the language then concerning the causes of the wounds that you would have included and perhaps excluded as well. Okay. Now, again, we're back to the same page of the exhibit that we looked at before; and for the patient 4543, you mentioned already the "vulnus explosiva." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then for the next witness down, are you able to read the indication of the cause of that person's wound?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe to some extent I can. It "V," and then "explosiva," I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you would have treated that, again, as what type of a wound?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a shelling -- a wounding from shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "Vulnus explosiva" is a shelling wound?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could move down the page just a little bit. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The entry for the witness at 4546, can you tell us what's indicated in terms of the nature of that individual's wound?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is "vulnus," V, again, "trans-sclopetarium," which was a term that was used for wounding acquired through gunshots.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So, again, that's terminology that you would use to place this person in the category of having been wounded by a gunshot; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just having a look at the individual immediately above this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could scroll up a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This individual, 4545, are you able to tell us what's indicated for that individual's condition?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say what is the meaning of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I wouldn't certainly include this person into the category of wounding from shelling or wounding from gunshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I don't see these familiar terms: "Vulnus explosiva," "trans-sclopetarium," or "sclopetarium."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, for this 4545, you did not include that or would not include that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not under the categories that we have just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, I believe the word read "partumerius," or something to that effect, and I believe a previous witness testified about this specific individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Shouldn't it be "parturience"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Trechsel. I believe that's correct. That's how I would read it, so it may be that this was a person who delivered a baby.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible. There were two victims reported who delivered babies, and one victim reported with a diagnosis that the person received artificial limb. So these are three cases unrelated to the wounding that we were looking at and studied in this project. These three unrelated cases were excluded from our study.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, getting back to the PowerPoint slide then. Let's talk about the overall totals of wounded that you arrived at based on your work: Absolute minimum now and more complete minimum numbers. Could you tell it us, first of all, the difference between those two as to these numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolute minimum number is, again, heavy underestimation. It is the number of 2.549 wounded persons. This number does not include the individuals that were reported on the missing pages. It is 465 individuals reported on these pages. We didn't have information about these persons, so they had to be excluded altogether from this minimum number. Nine persons of whom we didn't have enough information in the books were excluded from this number as well. Moreover, from this number a large group of records is excluded, specifically 2.844, for which there is no diagnosis explicitly reported in the war hospital books. So that is the major deficiency of the source that not for every patient the diagnosis is available. So the patients for whom the diagnosis is not available, not reported explicitly in the books, are excluded from the absolute minimum number. At the same time, we are convinced that this group for whom the diagnosis is unavailable should be considered as records that are of wounded persons. We studied these two groups, group of patients without a diagnosis and a group of patients with the diagnosis. We compared basic demographic distributions of these two groups, separately for civilians and for militaries, and we tested the differences between those two groups statistically. And the conclusion was that in terms of basic demographic characteristics, like age and sex distribution, and, of course, civilian-military distribution, these groups are not significantly different. There are no significant differences between these two groups. This, therefore, suggests that we should see the problem of not available diagnosis as a reporting problem. It is a deficiency of reporting and not of anything else. And based on this, we believe the group of 2.844 individuals without explicitly reported diagnosis should be included into the more complete absolute minimum number, which is reported on the slide as 5.393, 5.393. And this number is a better, more realistic estimate of the number of wounded persons in the siege of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And from a statistical point of the view, it's in your opinion correct, then, to include that figure, the 2.844 figure, in a calculation of a more complete absolute minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I have good reasons to include these records. As I said, we actually invested quite some time in comparing and studying these two groups, and I believe that these groups should be included in the more complete number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Springer, if I may. Does this mean, madam, that other "parturience," other persons who were there for entirely different reasons, might also be included in this figure? Because you take those that say nothing, and some in fact might have other causes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to stress that there were three cases -- three cases out of approximately 6.000 cases reported in the war hospital books that were unrelated to the wounding. So this is a negligible fraction, proportion of all patients. And based on this, I think it is safe to assume that unrelated cases are not represented practically, in practical terms, in the patients with no diagnosis reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I'm sorry -- if I must assist. I find it a bit difficult to understand your statement that there were three out of 6.000, when here you have 2.500 and some where no diagnosis, no cause is mentioned. Why do you still say they are all related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because as I said -- well, we have the entire population of patients, say approximately 6.000. We know that this population of patients is composed of two groups -- actually, of three groups: Unrelated cases, patients with diagnosis, and patients without the diagnosis. Now, first of all, if we calculate the proportion of unrelated cases in the entire population of patients of the hospital, it is 3 divided by 6.000. Approximately, of course, it is a negligible proportion. Of course I can apply this proportion to the patients of -- reported without diagnosis and I will end with a fraction, probably, of say one and a half person or something like that. I can subtract this person, but, in fact, would it really change what I'm trying to say? I'm trying to say something completely different. I'm trying to draw a conclusion about a large group of cases that I cannot include in the absolute number because an important information item is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understand the gist of it and can accept it, but would it not have been correct to compare the three to 2.549 and that would give the proportion among the cases with the known causes, and it would something different if you include the unknown. That would seem more correct to me, but maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, if we considered the patient with the diagnosis, any diagnosis, as one group, with the diagnosis as one group, then it would be correct to compare the three with the 2.549, and then, of course, the proportion would be higher because the denominator is smaller. But it would still be three persons as related to 2.549. So we are speaking of unrelated cases in the other group of a comparable size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, now we're at the final slide, and again what we've done is to put up the overall conclusions in respect of wounded persons in East Mostar. And if I could, as you did with the killed persons, perhaps you could just walk down these bullet points and give us your final conclusions and calculations.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, we just discussed the two numbers, minimum -- absolute minimum number, 2.549, which is based on the cases with the diagnosis reported and related to the siege of East Mostar. Well, there is a more complete estimate obtained by combining the patients without diagnosis with the records of patients with the diagnosis, which is 5.393. I call it a more complete estimate. And of course this estimate is still a minimum number because we are aware of cases that were never reported to the war hospital, and these would be the patients treated in out-patient facilities that were operating in this area during the siege. And there are patients reported on the missing pages 465 names who are not included in this number. There are 9 records excluded because they were too incomplete to work with them altogether. So these records are also out of this number. So this number is presented still as a minimum number. Well, the next line on the slide --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And excuse me -- yeah before you start talking about the percentages, just let me ask you this: In respect of all the percentages that appear now in these following bullet points that you're going to address, are these percentages that are reflected in the known cases, that is the 2549?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Those are cases --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- which you had a causes of injury was expressly included in the record?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These are percentages, proportions, obtained from the sample of the patients with diagnosis known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not exact proportions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that again nearly 82 per cent of those injuries were from shelling activity. 18 per cent from --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From gunshots and 44.5. Oh, this is another issue. Well, the 18 per cent of the injuries were from gunshots; right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the next line is related to the civilian military status. 44.5 per cent of the wounded persons were civilians. The civilians were reported in the war hospital books. The status was reported, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. And then as between male and female, men and women?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 42 per cent of wounded persons were women. Again, sex was reported in the source. And even if it wasn't, in some cases then a judgement was made based on the first name. Next conclusion is that almost all of the wounded persons, 97.7 per cent were Muslims. Again the assessment of ethnicity was made by native B/C/S speakers based on names of the patients. And on the other hand, it is not so surprising to see this high proportion because as we know the hospital was located in East Mostar. It was meant in the beginning as a hospital for the ABiH army, disregarding that it was meant for the army only. All patients were treated, not only militaries but civilians. Anybody who needed help was treated in this hospital. And the last conclusion is related to the age distribution of victims. 34.1 per cent of the wounded were at age 0 to 19 or older than 64 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all the questions I have, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question in relation to this. Did you also correlate these percentages to the population? You have just indicated, it's not surprising that a large per cent were Muslims. Perhaps the population were also 97 per cent Muslims. In that case, the distribution would be equal as a result. The same with the females. What percentage of the population were females? Did you do that correlation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would love to but we are speaking of East Mostar, a small area, into which a large number of the Muslim population moved in the early 1993, and there are reports. Several sources reported that the population increased up to maximal 55.000; whereas, normally the size of that population was much smaller. Well, what I'm trying to say is the population changed at the outbreak of the siege considerably, and I of course have no source that I could use for assessment of age and sex structure in this population. But regarding ethnicity, I think this is rather clear in my view, because it is known from other sources, not necessarily from the sources I studied, that the Muslim population was moving in early 1993 into this area, so I would expect that it was mainly if not exclusively the Muslim population that was living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a bit of a leading question. I'm sorry, I don't know how to -- well, let's say it like this: To have reliable percentages that are also significant, is it possible to have them if you do not have the comparative figures of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I work here in this study with a sample, sample of patients reported in the war hospital records. This is a very big sample. It is almost 6.000 records that we have reported in these books. So I believe it's a big sample, and I'm pretty sure that percentage 97.7 is significant. Statistically speaking, there is no doubt about it, I think. Whether it is a half of this population, 2.549 or 6.000, this relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've completed my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now have a break because it's time to have a break, and we shall resume with the cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understood, Mr. Kovacic wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In compliance with your instructions and further to the arguments we had two days ago on this issue, I wish to draw attention to the following: I feel that Mr. Praljak fulfils the conditions of your decision of the 10th of May to examine this expert witness. Your decision of the 28th of April, 2006 imposed for the first time certain limitations on the right of the accused to examine the witness himself directly, and the gist of that decision is that accused can put direct questions in exceptional circumstances. Those were the precise words of the decision. The practice after that has been for the Trial Chamber to apply this definition or this standard very extensively, without major limitations, and Mr. Praljak was allowed, almost without exception, to examine witnesses. On the 10th of May, 2007, your second decision was handed down, decision on the mode of interrogating witnesses, which in paragraphs 11 and 12 further develops the first decision from April 2006. And the limitations on the accused's ability to question witnesses were extended. There were additional limitations added on. It was decided that the Trial Chamber would apply the criteria from the first decision of April more strictly; that, as a rule, it will be counsel to examine witnesses; and under exceptional circumstances, with the approval of the Trial Chamber, the accused may question witnesses. In the next paragraph, paragraph 12, the term "exceptional circumstances" is clarified. It is stated here very precisely that special or exceptional circumstances have to do with events in which the accused participated personally, or they may be connected to topics of which the accused has specific knowledge. The term used was, to be quite precise, "issues for which the accused is specifically competent." The next condition imposed was that before the examination the, accused has to explain to the Chamber were he considers there are special circumstances in place. After that, new restrictions or more precise conditions were applied wisely and very extensively by the Trial Chamber; and almost without exception, Praljak was able to question witnesses, and only that is in areas that fell within the definition and the standard. With respect to the second decision, one Judge gave a separate opinion. On the 24th of August, the Appeals Chamber handed down a decision pursuant to an appeal by the Defence, and the appeal was rejected. Nothing new was added in that decision. Of course, grounds are given, but the gist is that the appeal was rejected. After the appeals decision, which confirmed the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 10th of May, the rules established in the decision of the 10th of May still apply. That's paragraphs 11 to 12. Pursuant to that decision, Praljak has the right to examine witnesses under the conditions I have just stated. He must explain to the Chamber why he feels he has a right to examine the witness, that these are events in which he personally participated, or topics for which he's specifically competent. In relation to the expert witness, who is testifying now and for whom I'm asking the Trial Chamber for permission for Praljak to question the witness himself, I wish to draw attention to the following elements: First of all, the expert witness is a demographer. The basic of discipline of demography is statistics. Statistics, as a scholarly discipline, is based primarily on mathematics. Praljak graduated from a university. He studied electronics, which includes an examination in mathematics 4, that's the highest level of mathematics studied at university. Praljak personally was involved in mathematics for a long time as a kind of hobby, and particularly in areas which are important for statistics. Praljak is the author of two books, one entitled "Refugees and displaced persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia." Parts of that book are in e-court under number 3D 01030. And the second book is "Crimes Committed against Croats in 1991 to 1995," and parts of the book are also in e-court. That's 3D 00322. And both these books include statistical analysis prepared by Praljak himself. Praljak also published two books, which Your Honours have not seen in e-court yet. One is called "Estimates of War Damages in Croatia," which again includes statistics, and the author is Praljak. And the other one is called "Aid Given by the Republic of Croatia to the Muslim Bosniak people and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991 to 1995," and again it includes a great deal of statistics and statistical analyses. Based on all this, it is evident that Praljak is specifically competent to deal with the topic that the witness is testifying about; therefore, the Chamber is moved to permit Praljak to examine the witness based on their decision of the 10th of May, in view of his specific competence. But I also wish to point out that he fulfils the second condition also, that he was directly involved in the events. Let's me remind you that there is an exhibit already in evidence of the 24th of July, 1993, where Praljak is mentioned as the commander who participated in all these events. I am referring to the data used by the expert, the data on certain facts and certain events on the ground which are data used for the analysis as entry data. So these are two reasons why I consider that Praljak should be granted this right. You have already heard that there is a lot of entry data here dealing with Mostar, the division of the town, positions, and Praljak is familiar with all of this because he was there. I wish to point out one more thing, and that is that were the Trial Chamber to insist on a restrictive application of the criteria set out on the 10th of May, which has not been the case hitherto, in view of the discussion two days ago, this would mean that those accused before this Tribunal who refused to have counsel, to appoint counsel, became a subject in their proceedings without being just an object; while those who did appoint counsel, like Praljak, do not have the right to examine witnesses themselves just because they have counsel. This would be an absurdity and, therefore, we move the Chamber to apply the standards set by the Chamber extensively rather than restrictively. I think these are important arguments. The Chamber will decide on the right of Praljak to examine the witness. He will, of course, adhere to those areas for which he's specifically competent and a little bit about the assumptions on which the analysis is based. The Defence teams are preparing to cross-examine the expert witness. The Prosecution disclosed the materials to us in June. In early July, we spoke to the accused, we as the Defence teams, and analysed the situation. My co-counsel and I are not familiar with mathematics, and we understand that a knowledge of mathematics can certainly contribute to a good cross-examination, and, therefore, Praljak took over the preparation. He consulted demographers during his vacation. And in view of this, because at that time, of course, the rule was being applied extensively and we did not doubt Praljak's right to cross-examine this witness. And some other accused have given him their time based on this understanding. Should there now be a turnaround in the practice, this would be highly detrimental to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just one minute. The Defence to which my colleague Mr. Kovacic referred as having given their time to General Praljak is, in fact, General Petkovic's Defence. It will be clear to Your Honours that preparations for the examination of this witness began from the point in time we learned that she would be testifying, and this was in July before the beginning of the summer break. Considering what could be done in half an hour of cross-examination, and bearing in mind the specific competence of General Praljak, which was has been described by Mr. Kovacic in detail, we agree with General Praljak that he should take over our time. We know that General Praljak spent his entire summer vacation preparing to examine this witness, and I know that he cooperated with my client in part while preparing for this examination. We, therefore, are willing to give our time to General Praljak; and for this reason, I ask that the rules which were in force in this courtroom when the decision was made to call this witness be applied, when the Defence teams agreed to prepare for the examination jointly and gave their time to General Praljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel having taken the floor, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, we oppose this application. The Trial Chamber's decision, now affirmed on appeal, provides that this is to occur only in exceptional circumstances. When every circumstance is exceptional, they're actually not exceptional any more. I don't know if I phrased that well. But certainly what we're seeing now is that, in our view, the Defence, the Accused Praljak, are really not being candid with the Pre-Trial Chamber about their true intentions. It's becoming evermore clear that this accused intends to conduct the lion's share of cross-examination himself, perhaps all of it, and that that is not an exceptional circumstance. Exceptional circumstances don't exist here as that term is defined in the Trial Chamber's decision. First of all, Mr. Praljak did not take part in any of the subject matter of the testimony of this witness. There aren't any events that he personally participated in, and so that condition is not met. Secondly, extraordinary circumstances might apply to areas about which he might be specifically competent, and we reject the assertion that this individual is specifically competent to -- in the sense that he is more competent than certainly his counsel to conduct this cross-examination. He's got highly qualified, skilled counsel who are, in our view, probably more competent than had him to conduct the examination. So those two factors have not been met here. Extraordinary circumstances do not exist in respect of this witness in particular; and indeed, Mr. President, if extraordinary circumstances are met in this situation and cross-examination of a demographer, expert, a statistical expert on reports concerning issues that this accused had nothing to do with in a personal capacity, then really every circumstance will be exceptional, and we might as well disregard the Trial Chamber's decision entirely. That's really what's being proposed here by the Defence, Mr. Praljak. It's going to be a recurring issue. He clearly intends to do this, not with just with this witness, not just with the last witness yesterday, but he intends to do it clearly with the coming witnesses, and, ultimately, hopes that the Trial Chamber will disregard its rulings and allow him, really, to run his own defence, while having the benefit of accused -- or counsel to sit in the courtroom with him. He wants it both ways, and he can't have it both ways, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall withdraw for a few minutes to deliberate, so please wait in the courtroom. Mr. Praljak, what would you like to add? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to add one more point. Except for my mathematical knowledge, which you yourself said that nobody can even deal with integrals in the courtroom, I'm a sociologist. I graduated from the Faculty of Sociology, and this goes hand-in-hand with demographic research: The creation of certain groups, comparisons, synchronising data, and consistency on the basis of one -- on the basis of which one makes conclusions, matching of samples, and so on. Those were part of my studies. And there was, of course, an agreement that I would examine this witness; and during the break, I consulted two leading demographic experts in Croatia, so that everything should be scientifically based here. And I think that, in my cross-examinations so far, I did strictly adhere to the facts and information which I have at my disposal and which are essential to the proceedings without going into some of the mistakes that perhaps I made at the beginning. I have learnt from them, so I just use facts, maps, tables, charts, and I wish through my cross-examination to contribute to the database in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I be allowed just to say one more sentence in response to the Prosecutor? The Prosecutor, at the end of his argumentation, said that Praljak cannot have it both ways; that is to say, his own -- the benefit of counsel and to run his own defence. So let me just remind you of the Rules and Statute, Article 21, which gives the accused the right both to defend himself and to have the benefit of counsel. So it's not either/or, it's both, and that has been clearly expressed in the Appeals request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will return in a few minutes. --- Break taken at 11.18 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber was seized of an application filed by Mr. Kovacic pursuant to the decision taken on the 10th of May, 2007, to entitle the Accused Praljak to put questions to the expert witness, a demographer. The Trial Chamber has also noted that this application was supported by Defence counsel of General Petkovic. The Trial Chamber also acknowledges that the Prosecution has objected to this procedure, submitting that the Appeals Chamber had confirmed the previous decision handed down by the Trial Chamber cannot permit in this particular case the accused to put questions. The Trial Chamber has deliberated on the matter and has unanimously deliberated on the matter, and I would like to recall all and everyone that in the future the Trial Chamber will apply the decision taken on the 10th of May, 2007. This decision has been upheld by the Appeals Chamber. And prior to that date, practice would have it that in certain cases questions were put, but this will no longer be the case, and the Trial Chamber will apply the decision of the 10th of May, 2007, to the letter. In this particular case, the Trial Chamber, after having heard both parties and after having heard the Accused Praljak, acknowledges that, as far as this particular hearing is concerned, the Accused Praljak has prepared some of the issues, technical issues, together with two demographers. In addition, it seems that his counsel had decided that the cross-examination would be conducted by his client. In addition, the Accused Praljak has written a few books on the subject, provides statistical data, and, therefore, may be competent, technically speaking, and meet the requirements set out in the decision. The Trial Chamber, therefore, unanimously authorises the Accused Praljak to put questions, and this is an exceptional circumstance. And the Trial Chamber would like to remind everybody present that the Accused Praljak will have the 30-minute allotted time in addition to the 30 minutes given to him by Petkovic's Defence counsel. We shall now bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to inform you that the Defence of Mr. Stojic has given its examination time for the examination of this witness to Mr. Praljak as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the record, we also cede our time to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have resumed our hearing; and pursuant to a decision handed down by the Trial Chamber, the Accused Praljak will now put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you for your decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I don't see a transcript on my screen. If somebody can help me rearrange. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it correct, madam, that in your analysis, you have something that is called a source of information, which is indubitable, clear, and so on, and created groups and samples that can be created on different grounds? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I use sources of information. They might be complete, or they might be samples.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd like now to see how you created different groups. Among others, you had a group which was the number of Muslims in what you refer to as the eastern side of Mostar, and you established that group in the following manner: According to your statement, this cluster was devised by you on the basis of the fact that you asked people with their names and surnames to tell you which ethnic group they belonged to, which nationality, because you didn't have this column, and then you recorded it subsequently based on the names that people told you were Muslim or Bosniak names. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sources and groups are perhaps two different things. Sources is where the information I use in my study come from, and the groups as the Muslims that you mentioned are, indeed, groups of records in these sources. Regarding the ethnicity you are referring to, I am not exactly sure what source you are speaking about, but I would guess it is Mostar war hospital records, because it was the only source in which ethnicity was assigned on the basis of names. If you can confirm that we are talking about the war hospital records.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about records from the war hospital in which ethnicity was not recorded; and then, subsequently, when you looked into subsequent data, you arrived at nationality or ethnic group on the basis of names, because local people, judging by the names, said, "Yes, this is a Muslim name. It's Mustafa, which means a Muslim name," and so on. So is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar war hospital records, indeed, ethnicity wasn't reported, and a group of B/C/S speakers, native B/C/S speakers, assigned the ethnicity based on names. However, it's good to remember that this is a very special source, Mostar war hospital regards. This is the hospital that was meant to treat the population of East Mostar, and East Mostar population was known to be composed of mainly, almost exclusively, Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, in response to a question from the Prosecution, you qualified certain things. You said that certain things were known and so on. Now, I'd like to ask you to refrain from explaining what you knew or what was known and what was not known, what was your source, whether you were in Mostar or not. I asked you a specific question: Nationality, ethnic group from the war hospital records, the source. You created that on the basis of the fact that somebody told you that this name and that name were Muslim names. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it in my testimony. Ethnicity was created by native B/C/S speakers. I didn't do that, neither my section, others in my section, didn't do that. We received this created item from the investigations team. This is -- this is what I said, and this is what I confirm. However, I can't separate entirely from what I know about my sources, as I believe the qualitative analysis and assessment of sources is a very important step in producing numbers of victims in the conflict. And I will use the qualitative knowledge of sources in this testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, we'll get to that. Something that is referred to in scholarly work was footnotes. So we'll get to the footnotes and statement of sources. We'll come to that in due course. I'll ask you whether scholarly work has footnotes and whether you have to name your sources in the footnotes. But you're not talking about source here or I'm not talking about sources. You use the first person singular in your work, in your report, and it does not explain the sources. You speak as if you are well aware of those facts and that information. So now I'd like to clarify the quality of the facts and assertions you arrived at when you said which people were Muslims and which aren't. Now, in the 1991 statistical data, the town of Mostar, and that statistical data has already been supplied to the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] We did not get the answer from the witness. You didn't do the determination. You said it was B/C/S speakers who actually made the determination. So I was waiting for some additional information on this, and Mr. Praljak moved on to other things.
