So this is my question: The people who helped you to say that, for example, person number 4543 was of Muslim ethnicity; who said that to you? Could you please tell us who came up with this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I received electronic version of this data from hospital books. In the spreadsheet that we received, ethnicity was already included; and from the work log I received, together with the spreadsheet, I read that native B/C/S speakers obtained or estimated ethnicity based on the names. And these native B/C/S speakers were not people I know or I knew. They were people employed by the investigations team, probably part of the investigations team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So if we go into detail, you obtained by mail these lists; and in the spreadsheet, the ethnic background was noted. And you told us that the people who actually came up with the ethnicity are the people working for the OTP; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding, yes. These are B/C/S speakers, native speakers, but working for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, in your statement, you mention the fact that the death registers in February 2001 was given over to you by the agency from -- AID agency from Sarajevo. Now, my question to you is: Do you know what work the AID agency in Sarajevo was involved in?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, may I just intervene? In the record it is AID, the abbreviation of the agency A-I-D, capital letters. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know what the organisation dealt with, that one in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see the question -- [French on English channel] -- to the fact how I obtained the death registries, and I did not obtain the death registries from the AID agency. I was provided with these death registries by the investigations team, OTP. I didn't collect these registries myself. I usually do collect my sources, but not in this case. And it is possible that the team obtained these registries from AID. I do know what AID is doing. This is an agency doing intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam Witness, Doctor, I am strictly adhering to what you said, and here it says that: "In 2001, in the month of February, I handed over by the AID agency in Sarajevo." Now, you claim, you're saying - and we'll come back to this because I'm not clear on it - it's your scholarly work, your expertise, and this is what you say, and now you say you don't know and so on. Now, I'm going to ask you very precise questions. I'll try and get through this as quickly as possible, so please give me short answers to my questions. Say, "Yes, I do know," "No, I don't know," with few comments. In 1991, the town of Mostar, according to the statistical data of the 1991 census, it had a total of 75.865 inhabitants. Of that number, people who declared themselves as Croats, there were 21.795 of those, 25.929 declared themselves as Muslims; 14.142 declared themselves as Serbs; 11.555 declared themselves as Yugoslavs; and there was a category of others, 2.444. So they declared themselves, as far as nationality is concerned, 61.000-odd or 81.85 per cent; 13.999 persons did not declare themselves, or 18.5 per cent. Tell me now, please, with what right did somebody later on change the -- the ethnicity of almost 20 per cent of people who had not declared themselves on an ethnic basis, did not declare their ethnicity. That's my first question. And my second question that follows on from that is this: Was a cluster or group created of ethnicities, ethnic groups, in the hospital registers and death registers on the basis of the fact that every "Mujo," every person called "Mujo" or "Mustafa," was proclaimed to be a Muslim, and that this was a very rough estimation. Because regardless of the fact that the person's name might have been "Mujo" or "Mustafa," this person could have declared himself as a Croat, a Serb, or not declared himself at all?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see three questions in your question. And, well, first one is related to AID. I would like that you would show me where, in my report, I say that I obtain the death registers from the AID. As far as I remember, I was provided the death registries by the investigations teams -- team. This is my one comment. Second comment, you are referring to figures on the ethnic composition in Mostar. Again, I would like to hear what is the source, if it is the population census or if it is published data. It would help us if we could understand this. And then, finally, there is the ethnic definition, ethnicity issue. It's the third issue that you raised. So if you can please help me first with the reference to my report source as the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak will help you, but Ms. Alaburic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, might I be of permission with respect to AID? The witness mentions this in her expert report under P 9835 of killed persons with regard to the siege of Mostar, and the figure was quoted in part 2, the Mostar death registers in chapter 4 or paragraph 4 in the Croatian text. That is on line 6 of that fourth paragraph, and I quote: "The death registers in February 2001 were handed over by the AID agency from Sarajevo to the OTP," and then the sentence continues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I see this reference to AID. And, well, if it is in the report, then this is the source how the team obtained it. But I'm saying, once again, I obtained the death registries directly from the investigations team. But perhaps it is important to mention on this occasion that death registration is part of vital events registration. In every country, every death is registered in the death register. There is a period of three days within which -- after death, within which the death needs to be reported to the authorities. So even though the AID was involved in providing these death registries to the OTP, I believe as a source, as a source as such, the nature of the source has nothing to do with intelligence. It is just reporting of deaths in a population. So I can't see what impact can it have that the AID provided this source to the OTP in general. Okay. So the answer I understand to the source of your statistics is the book published by the Croat authorities, the figures -- census figures published by the Crostat in 1995, and the question is related to ethnicity. If you can please repeat it, I would be happy to hear it again. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: First of all, madam, in view of the fact that you had the right to say all had this before, but you are a demographer. Do you agree that you're not an expert on what AID was doing, what its intentions were, and so on? Do you agree that it's not part of your expert opinion whether the information provided to you by the AID are reliable or not? It's just a simple fact that they were provided by the AID. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree I am an expert on demographics in this case, and I am entitled to have my opinion as a demographic expert on the sources I used. And death registries, this is my expert opinion, is a source that is usually available in every population, and this is a statistical source and a good source. And the source, as such, is a not compiled by any intelligence agency. It is compiled by authorities who are responsible for registration of vital events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I don't mean to interrupt General Praljak, but the three hours were allocated to all of the Defence, and I feel that I'm being disadvantaged here because the witness is being non-responsive deliberately. The question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may make my record, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President, it's not the view --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am entitled to make my record. If you look at the -- the question was whether she was competent to testify about what AID does in their intentions. You have a long explanation afterwards without responding. Furthermore, she was asked earlier by what authority, by what authority, she could change the names. Again, long explanation or no explanation. What I'm saying is that the witness is a Ph.D.. She's testified at least seven or eight times. She's a professional witness. She works for the Office of the Prosecution. She is an employee of the office of the Prosecution, and she should, therefore, I think, be more forthcoming and shorter with the answers. She can answer the questions very directly. I think that this is a deliberate attempt to eat up the Defence time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be brief. This tenancy to mix, introduce argument, points very well known, very effective at times from Defence, arguing the witness is biased, she's being non-responsive. Fine. Those are legitimate arguments to be made, you know, all the time. Not as to this witness, in my view, but it's all argument. Counsel can make those arguments as much as he likes to the Trial Chamber when the time comes for arguing what the Trial Chamber, in the view of the parties, should attach to this witness's testimony at the closing arguments. But now to have these sorts of accusations flying around in the courtroom, while the witness is here, is quite another thing. It's not appropriate cross-examination, and it, frankly, wastes everyone's time. In our view, the witness is doing her best to answer the compound questions that are being put to her by a non-attorney now, who is being allowed to cross-examine an expert. He's not asking her a question. He's asking her three questions in the course of rather lengthy paragraphs. So if perhaps Mr. Praljak could phrase his questions in a way that a skilled advocate would do, enabling her to give measured answers to limited questions, it would facilitate the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just give you an example. Mr. Praljak asked about receiving information from AID. He said "you." She then said, "No. It won't me; it was some other folks," and so on and so forth. Lengthy explanation, no concrete answer, and then you, Mr. President, had to ask a series of questions, and, finally, we get a confession from the witness who says, "yes." And then it is Ms. Alaburic who has to point, and then she, says, "Where is this?" It's in her own report, a report that she signed, that she did, . So my question is: Why do we have to waste three or four minutes on something where she said "yes." That's my point. It is not arguing. What I am saying is: We have three hours collectively, and so these sort of answers affect my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, when you're asking a question, don't put three questions in one, please. Just ask one question; wait for your answer, yes, no, or maybe a bit lengthier; and then move on to the second question. So please proceed step-by-step. It will save time. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. Since the record is because mischaracterised, the question was whether she was handed the records in a personal capacity. That's how I understand it. Now the report says they were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, so that's quite a different thing. And I think that it's unfair to suggest that she's evasive or has confessed to some sort of incorrect or false answer before. Simply not true. It's only based upon spin and mischaracterisation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please proceed, and please make sure that your questions are short and extremely clear and straightforward. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is very simple: If the information I have quoted from the census of 1991 says that 81.5 per cent of the population of the town of Mostar declared their ethnic affiliation and 18.5 did not, my question is on the basis of what analysis did you ascribe an ethnic affiliation to 20 per cent of those who did not declare themselves by ascribing to them ethnicity based on their name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can answer. It is a very clear question, very straightforward, and I'm sure that the answer will be very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In the publication by Crostat, ethnicity is reported separately as Muslims, Croats, Serbs, Yugoslavs, and as far as I remember, are other ethnicity and unknown, something like that. So is this unknown ethnicity 18 per cent? I'm just making sure that I understood you correctly. It is really a very high per cent. As far as I know, it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it is a larger group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is very clear. On what basis? Now she can say, "This is a statistical methodology that we use." That's the question. The question is very clear. What gives her the right, that was the question, to impose these other nationalities? Is it something that demographers do on all occasions? Is this something is they have to do because of the extraordinary circumstances? That was the question. That is the essence of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Karnavas seems to be conducting this cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is just one thing, please. This witness is under oath. She made a solemn declaration. She is now in the hands of justice and is no longer connected with the OTP and, therefore, will undergo cross-examination. If she's in a difficult situation, don't necessarily stand up to come and help. However, the question is very simple. It's a mathematical question. 20 per cent of the Mostar population did not declare itself as being Croats or Muslim. We have 20 per cent; and we know that among these 20 per cent, we know that 11.000, more than 11.000, said they were Yugoslavs. Of course, they were either probably Muslim or Croat, and scientifically, no one can challenge the fact that, in 1991, there is a chart regarding Mostar with ethnic composition in percentage. So you're a demographer and then you carry out your work after -- from these figures, but the question that comes to mind is: Where are these 11.000 Yugoslavs? What has become of them? How come you or who were before you, how did they introduce these Yugoslavs in the total population? Did you decide they were Muslims or Croats? That's the question asked, and we need an answer. Tell us, "I don't know," "I know," but we need an answer. This is a statistical element that we need to understand; otherwise, everything becomes extremely approximate with this 20 per cent margin of unknown, because 20 per cent of the sample is not determined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I must say I disagree that 20 per cent is unknown. That is my expert opinion because Yugoslav is an ethnic group that is completely different from Muslim, Serb or a Croat. It is a group in itself, and it is part of the 20 per cent; and in this 20 per cent, we have Yugoslavs and others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But don't play on words, please. You are saying that Yugoslavs is a group in itself. Maybe statistically it is, but these 11.000 Yugoslavs have some kind of ethnic background. That's the whole problem. And when statistically they're distributed into two ethnic backgrounds according to your work, the next question is: How did you move them into one or the other category?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to say that, as a matter of fact, I agree with the witness's view that the group of Yugoslavs and the group of Muslims, they are two different issues and two different groups. The group of Yugoslavs, they name themselves. They call themselves "Yugoslavs" because when the census was taken, they didn't want to belong to, say, Croat or Serb or whatever ethnicity or national group. But it was mainly a question of citizenship, if I may say so, in former Yugoslavia - and I hope that those who had lived there would confirm this - and it was not a question of ethnicity. And that is why I share the view expressed by the witness, that whenever there was a finding that according to the names they were Muslims, it could be accepted. It is another question if they themselves previously declared themselves Yugoslavs or Croats or Serbs or whoever, whatever. And for me also, frankly speaking, the shrapnels, the shelling, the snipers' bullets did not make any difference between Yugoslavs and Serbs and Muslims and Croats, and that is why I would accept the groupings what the witness used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, in light of what was said, can you please proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I partly agree with His Honour. I agree that the Yugoslavs are a separate group. And we are not questioning here that victims are victims and that everybody's affected in the same way by a shell or a bullet, but the calculation of the number of Muslims hit by the shelling is at issue. If 20 per cent of the population did not declare their ethnicity, they are transforming 20 per cent of the population into a certain ethnic group based on their names and then calculating the percentage of Muslims. If the percentage of Muslims hit on the west bank had been not calculated, I would not have put this question. The error can be more than 20 per cent, if they are transferred from one category to another.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So my question is: Based on what scientific analysis did you conclude based on people's names what ethnic group they belonged to, because this is a piece of information that belongs to each individual, to each individual's declaration in the census. You say, "We did it this way." Let's move on. Just say that and I'll move on. I'll be satisfied with your reply, and then my time is running out so I do wish to move on. So please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you that ethnicity is a self-perceived item and this is how it was reported in the census, and we didn't have these kind of reports. It is an estimate that we made of ethnicity, but perhaps it our discussion will become easier if I will say that our objective was to measure casualties among the Bosniak population. The choice of sources was to measure the casualties among the Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please. Thank you very much. I have received the reply to my question. My next question is: Based on the information available, did you arrive at the basic group? In other words, in that part of Mostar municipality which was under BH army control, what was the population? What was the number of men? What was the number of women? What number of people were there in each season of the year? So did you have this basic set, this basic group, of the population on BH army-controlled territory, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that territory controlled by the ABiH army is East Mostar. This is what you're referring to. And I said earlier today, I didn't have the size of the population in East Mostar. There exists estimates from 35.000 to 55.000, and that is all we know. There is no statistical record of this population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Wouldn't it have been simpler if you had said, "We did not create this set"? Let's move on. My next question is: Within this set that you did not create, did you conduct any kind of analysis as to mortality in the pre-war period? If you have a set of citizens of Mostar between 35 and 55.000 in number, and based on information you could have gathered, you could have said the natural mortality rate in this set is such-and-such: Traffic accidents, murders, suicides, and so on accounts for so many. Injuries are such-and-such. Mortality in hospitals during surgeries which went wrong is such-and-such, and so on. Did you calculate how many people died of natural causes because of illness, disease, or accident, so as to have reference, a set to refer to of people who had died of natural causes in that area? Did you do that analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that, in my reports, I didn't deal with natural causes, and there is no reference made to natural mortality in Mostar or in a smaller area within the Mostar municipality before the conflict period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, in that basic set, did you analyse the mortality according to the criteria that I have set out, yes or no, madam, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what is the basic set to you. I said I didn't study mortality, pre-war morality, in Mostar, or in a smaller area within Mostar, mortality from natural causes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are traffic accidents, murders, suicides, death during childbirth, or surgery, are all these natural causes to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are causes. These are external, I would put it this way. These are natural causes. What we mean are natural causes is age-related causes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] My questions, Your Honours, are very simple.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm trying very hard to put simple questions. Every population in Paris, London, or Zurich has a statistic that say so many people die of old age a year, so many are murdered each year, so many commit suicide each year, so many die in traffic accidents, and so on and so forth. Did you conduct such an analysis among the population of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. It wasn't my objective.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. You said here today that there was an unexpected rise in mortality in September and October 1993 -- August and September, that is, 1993. And you say that the expected mortality rate would not have been so high because in winter and in the autumn or in spring more people die. There is a higher mortality. Do you have this information for the city of Mostar? It could have been found in all the previous statistical information. The reason I'm asking this is that Mostar is a very warm town. In summer, temperatures rise as high as 40 to 45 degrees. So can you transfer statistical data referring to Europe to a town such as Mostar which has no snow in winter, which doesn't have cold winners, but has very hot summers? So did you analyse the mortality, the pre-war mortality, of the citizens of Mostar by season of the year?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't do this for Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You used the original data from the Mostar hospital and the record of deaths, and then you improved that by also using the military records of those killed in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question is as follows: Apart from soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did others participate in combat, in military activities, that is; for example, the civilian protection, for example, carrying food to the front lines and so on, without being recorded in these military records? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that these are set on special lists, the military lists. Not everybody, not the Civil Defence is there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the end of the war, during the time of privatisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all those who had participated in the war, either in the civilian protection, the civilian police, or in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had vouchers distributed to them. These were vouchers they could use to acquire shares in publicly opened companies. Did you obtain the lists of those who were issued with vouchers because they had taken part in military activities but were not soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and did you compare those lists with the military records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't use this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When creating the set of killed soldiers and civilians, did you calculate in the civilian police which, as we know, wore military uniforms when they walked around Mostar, but they are not included in the list of those killed as members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? So did you collect lists of civilian policemen killed in the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Did you look at the number of members of the 4th Corps which were located on the territory of the town of Mostar? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said what military sources I used. These were the lists provided by the Ministries of Defence of both entities. Well, whether the 4th Corps soldiers were reported in these lists, I wouldn't exactly know, but I would guess that they were. This is just a guess.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 3D 01065, 3D 01065. That is a book published by General Drekovic, the commander of the 4th Corps after General Pasalic left. So it's 3D 01065, and open to the page where there is a table. It's 1857. The page is 3D 26-1857. There's a table there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What page is this? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's on your screen. It lists the numbers of those killed in 1992 and up in 1993 up to the 19th of January 1994, and the upper table refers to units of the 4th Corps and the second to the 4th and 6th Corps. Did you know that the 4th and the 6th Corps were one and the same corps, the 4th Corps, up to the 19th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I know this? I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, just give me a simple answer. Say, "I don't know." You don't have is to justify yourself. You're not the accused. I'm the accused here. Just say you don't know, and I can move on.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Now, take a look at the following data. Up until the 19th of January, 1993, and part of 1994, 579 people were killed, members of the 4th Corps, and 1.168 people were wounded. Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it obviously does.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my question to you is this: Do you know that, in addition to the 4th Corps units, at the time that you talk about, August, September, there were additional units added from the 1st Corps, from Sarajevo, in the fighting around Mostar? Do you know that some other units, Zuka's men or whatever, that other units arrived in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you looked at the table referring to 1993, did you make an analysis of those who were killed up until the 9th of May from this corps, based on records that I'm sure exist, and those who were killed after the 9th of May, 1993? Did you make that record?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the table from the book?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't make any analysis with this table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers of the 4th and 6th Corps had together? What was its strength together?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I don't. I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. If the -- when the soldiers came back from the front line after doing their shift, do you know whether they changed into civilian clothes, and when if it they were taken to hospital, they would be registered as civilian deaths or members of the civilian police or soldiers who came to the hospital wearing civilian clothes? Did you look at that kind of thing? Do you have any information about that, that in the war hospital records they had records of that nature?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they didn't have record of clothes and changing the clothes in particular; not in hospital books.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. In your -- among your data, you say that 5.393 persons were wounded soldiers according to the war hospital Mostar records, and you cover this until the 20th of April, 1994, and that is 380 days -- 382 days. Now, if 5.000-odd is divided by the number of days -- if 5.393 persons is divided by 380 days, the average number of persons arriving in hospital per day is 14. Is that right? So 5.000-odd divided by 380 gives us the sum of 14.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: One correction. 5.393 is not wounded soldiers. It is all wounded persons, a part of them being soldiers, but being civilians. Well, you made some calculations, and you are telling us the number of persons arriving on average is 14. Perhaps it is correct. I didn't do the calculation right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, I didn't say that they were soldiers. I said they were patients during that period of time. Now, if we assume that number can vary twice or three times in any given day, then my question is this, and we're talking about the quality of the evidence or the lack of quality of the records --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not evidence, records. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, if 14 people are admitted to hospital, is that a small number which allows the doctors to write down the reasons for which the people were brought to the hospital in the first place. So it says vulnus explosiva as the diagnosis. That would be correct because these are qualified doctors who were able to write the diagnosis for each person, because the number of people admitted to hospital wasn't that great. It was, on average, 14 per day.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was, on average, 14, if you are right, of course, and some days it was higher than that. And, well, I believe 14 per day, if we assume it is correct, it is certainly a possible thing to do, to record the details of all 14 people. But there is, I understand, a group of people that perhaps were never registered in these books as well, as knowing the source.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, madam. I might come back to certain issues, but as my time is running out -- well, it hasn't run out yet. I don't want to use Mr. Karnavas's time, so I'll go through this quickly. Would you take a look at your report on the deaths as a result of the conflict. According to the war hospital records and the death registers -- would you take a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give us a page number perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll start off with page 1 where you say that as a place of death the sources usually quote municipalities. Those are the last two lines on the first page. So that it is impossible to establish which deaths occurred in East Mostar and which occurred outside that area. Do you state that loud and clear there on page 1 and part of page 2? The first line on page 2.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember what I wrote. Generally, sources report the municipality of that, and there is also a place of death which is not always available. In this particular sources we also had this problem, especially with the deaths registers, that not every record was available in terms of a specific place of death. For many only municipality was reported as a place of death, which was not good enough to study and to include in our absolute numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you consider that the data from the death registers are more precise than the data in the Mostar hospital?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to personal details they are. Not when this comes to details about the death.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now turn to page 632, please. 632. That's the Croatian version. I can't give you the English page number. It's the portion in table 1. After table 1 where you address the death registers and what is contained in them. Table 1, please. It's number 4 in the English version. After table 1 you say the following: "Only some places can be classified as being East Mostar, whereas the other places can't be recorded under that column so that places that have not been designated as East Mostar need not necessarily be outside the East Mostar area; although, the category, East Mostar is not quoted, and this refers to deaths outside the area of East Mostar. Data from East Mostar for some reason have not been designated as East Mostar. They have also been included into this category." Now, can you tell me, please, what were the reasons that you decided that those which were not designated at East Mostar you should include in the East Mostar category? Could you explain your reasons for that, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- first of all, I didn't include in my analysis any deaths of which I couldn't be sure that they were in East Mostar. So all the deaths of which I either didn't know, or I did know that they were from outside East Mostar, these were excluded. They are not in the minimum numbers. So there is no reasons that I would include these deaths. I didn't include these deaths.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. So the minimum numbers are those numbers which because of sentences like this that you use can say certain numbers either in the war hospital records or the death registers. So the minimum numbers are the actual numbers, the most reliable numbers, that they are scientifically the most reliable numbers, these minimum numbers. Can we say that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I'm saying in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Now would you turn to page -- or, rather, to table number 3 on page 1032 of the Croatian text. It is page 7 of the English. Take a look at that. And you say judging by everything, the number of deaths due to all the different causes, including natural causes as well in certain cases, although we noted earlier on that you didn't research that, recorded in space and time contained in the indictment was 773, and this related to the overall area of Capljina, Jablanica, Mostar, Prozor, and Stolac. And you have table 3 with 773 deaths, including, as you say, a certain number of natural deaths. But is that the correct table? Is that right? For five municipalities the total is 773 deaths. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is at this stage just a table reporting on some intermittent results, but it is not a table that should be taken as a table with minimum absolute numbers for Mostar. It includes many more municipalities and Mostar as a whole, not only East Mostar. You should rather refer to the next table, table number 4, in which these seven -- the number for Mostar 524 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please. I'm reading your own words, and these are your words. The number of deaths all in all recorded within the space and time comprised in the indictment was 773. Table 3. And there you go on to enumerate 11, Capljina; Jablanica, 227; Mostar, 135; Prozor, 5; and a total of 374, and then you have known and unknown quantities. But this is 773, a total of 773. And then you go on to say the total number for the Mostar municipality is 524 cases of which only 373 cases satisfy the strict demands of relevance and relating to the siege of Mostar. That is to say those deaths which occurred in East Mostar in the period between May 1993 to April 1994. Now, madam, are those your words? Is that what you said? And then we'll see what follows. But is this the demand for relevance and reliability, this figure 773?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are reading section 2, which is summary of the source, and there is another section which contains final statistics. If you need final numbers, you should go to section on final statistics and not to go through the summary of the source. I am summarising the source in order to make sure that everybody understands that I'm not taking the entire source, that I exclude large parts of this source, and I only take a small group of record of which I know they are relevant, and the small group of record is 373.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, now take a look at the following page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we need to have a break now. We'll have a 20-minute break and resume after that and go on until a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe Mr. Stringer want to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we may be in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have used up 47 minutes so far out of the two hours which were allocated to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doctor, madam, let's continue. On page 10, underneath table 3, you say the following: The real causes of death were these 773 cases for these municipalities that you mention and which are relevant for the indictment are stated as following: Violent death linked to the conflict, violent death perhaps linked to the conflict, natural death, unknown causes killed by gunshot, shelling, murder, suicide, et cetera, all these other causes. And we can add to that traffic accidents and so on, or death caused by other reasons. Now let's move on to page 11 and table 4. You have a table there and you say East Mostar. And you say that this is -- these are valid cases from Mostar judging by the date and place of birth, and you say that 91 persons for 1993 and 1994. 91 persons that the place of death is not known, but 373 persons do have a known place of death; and then you say this number of 373 recorded in East Mostar during the siege in May -- from May 1993 to April 1994, considers to be relevant and valid for the needs of analysing the fatalities of the siege, the victims of the siege. Do you stand by that statement? What we're not challenging, what is from the base of date that you have at your disposal, things are not challenged.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these 373 are related to the siege at Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move on to table 6 on page 14, page 9 of the English. And you go on to elaborate, and we have comparative data there. In table 6, cause of death as a result of the siege, siege-related deaths reported in the Mostar war hospital books and in the Mostar death registries; and then you say gunshots 49, shelling 214, unknown 209, wounding 0. With the death registers, we have 6 who were killed, natural deaths 11, shelling 14, unknown 333. 333 unknown. Can you explain to us - and we can stay with these figures - whether under "Unknown" in the war hospital, was it really unknown? And if you made a new group or looked at a new group or cluster, hadn't you perhaps forgotten that the physicians did not write the cause of death -- or rather, did write the cause of death. So doctors are to be trusted. So if somebody dies in hospital, they can know the wounds that caused death. So how do you know -- how could they have wrote that, in 209 cases, the cause of death was unknown? Because if they were killed as a result of gunshot wounds or shelling, you would see injuries on the body -- or rather, they would see injuries on the body.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the 209 unknown cases reported from war hospital books, what is known is that these were violent deaths and deaths were because of wounding. What is unknown is unknown whether it was a wounding by a shell or it was a wounding by a gunshot. So here they are reported as unknowns.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. How come you're able to claim that it is unknown whether they -- this death was caused by shelling or gunshots, when you say that they have three ways of determining this, the traces on the body, vulnus sclopetarium, whether it was and entrance/exit wound, or wounds of shelling? I don't see that you studied that the unknown persons died of wounding if this was not recorded. So how do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed problems of reporting in the war hospital books; and I said, and I stand behind it, that the source is incomplete and many records lack the diagnosis. At the same time, we know that this is a very special source. These are records from a war hospital located in the siege area and that was established to treat patients, victims of the siege, and who was treated in the hospital were, except for three cases of whom we know were unrelated, were cases all related to the siege and were victims of wounding by shell and gunshots. So these are the reasons that I know that these deaths of which we don't know the particular cause. But let me finish. We know that these are violent deaths related to the siege.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll come to discuss the siege later on. I'll ask you something about the siege. It's a term that can be disputed, but I'm not clear on anything now. From the fact that you know something exactly - and it's these three cases that I'm referring to - it would emerge that based on the fact that you know something exactly, then you can conclude that it's another group. Where in the war hospital records for the 209 persons does it say that they died a violent death, if we see that we have 214 for shelling and 49 gunshots? So what else is there that is unknown, if we do know that we have 214 cases of death through shelling and 49 through gunshot wounds? So the doctor says he died, that there was shelling, and so-and-so died; and then under the "Unknown," you say that those unknown were also violent deaths. What are your grounds for asserting that these unknown were due to violent deaths as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the fact that the patients treated in the hospital were wounded persons. This is what is in the data. There is a group of patients of whom the diagnosis is unknown; but for all those for whom the diagnosis is known, and who can be reliably to be considered as a sample of all patients of the hospital, we see that these are wounded persons. And three cases, unrelated cases, were all unrelated cases we saw in the data.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please. We're not here to perform statistical exercises and training. We're here to establish the facts. If a doctor -- if the doctors say there were 49 deaths due to gunshot wounds and 214 due to shelling and some unknown ones, 209, then please tell me, when you looked at these unknown, they must have died from shelling and gunshot wounds, must they not? How else?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the deaths that are listed here in the table as unknown, 209, we know that these are violent deaths of people who first got wounded and died in hospital of their wounds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How? Where does it say that? Where is that written? Did they fall down the stairs? Were they perhaps injured when handling weapons themselves? Where does it say? Because it says "Unknown." These are not statistical exercises. I'm not your student. Here it says "Unknown," where you say, "We know full well." So tell the Trial Chamber: How do you know full well? It's a simple question. If you don't want to answer, I can move on, but then don't say we know. What is the basis for the "we know"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for the "we know" is the nature of the data and the nature of the source. It is not just a regular hospital that treats any patient of any condition. This is a war hospital and treats patients who are victims of fighting. This is so simple, and this is one thing. Another thing is: Well, I had the opportunities to see some videos and some pictures of the hospital during the siege and of what kind of patients were treated in this hospital. It only confirms what I know about the source.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, at the beginning -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And Their Honours can look at Dr. Rajkov's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: -- you quoted yourself: "50 per cent of our patients were civilians," he says, and this is something that you quoted. Is that correct, that you accepted Dr. Rajkov's statement to the effect that that war hospital was the only hospital; and as the only hospital that was able to undertake surgery, they took in the population which was between 33 and 35.000? So, if there were fractures, bone fractures, falling downstairs, traffic accidents, this hospital would take all of these people in. And the fact that you did not look into these and study them, you say it's the unknown, because this is a war hospital and I saw pictures. So this 209, is that anything other -- do you have grounds to state that this is anything other than just unknown?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in terms of reported diagnosis, I don't have diagnosis for these cases. What I do know of these cases, these are deaths in war hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That will do. Unknown, right. In table 7, you have the distribution according to the months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing for clarification. You're talking about a war hospital, and you draw conclusions out of this. I was quite surprised to see earlier this lady who came obviously came to give birth. So maybe this hospital's main calling was to treat all the injured in the conflict, but also used as a general hospital. And because it was also used as a general hospital, other kinds of patients could come to get treatment, patients who were not direct victims of the conflict. Somebody who suddenly has a heart attack just one kilometre from this hospital will be taken to this hospital. And if he dies in the hospital after the heart attack, maybe the cause may be unknown. He's not shot by a sniper and not caught in an explosion. So you told us that you saw some video and so on, but I'd like to know the following: Is this just a war hospital whose only calling is to treat the military and to treat the victims of the conflict, or is it a hospital that has a double purpose; military, on the one hand, and also civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was another hospital in Mostar in the west part of Mostar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Mostar east, not west.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In East Mostar, this hospital was established as a war hospital for the ABiH army, and it was established at the outbreak of the siege in East Mostar, and the main purpose was to provide medical services to the wounded soldiers, I believe. But, at the same time, it was the only hospital in the area and a very poorly equipped hospital. And, well, it is understandable that, if somebody happened to give birth in the siege period and didn't have any other opportunity, they would come to this hospital, of course, and this is what we see. There are three records of unrelated cases in the hospital, but this is all what we see in the records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's have a theoretical example. Let's imagine that a child under 12 suddenly has appendicitis turning into peritonitis, and, of course, this child is sent to the hospital immediately, this hospital. Unfortunately, this child dies; but then, in that case, which category would this child fall into statistically, the unknown? What category would you put this person in, this child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if the diagnosis would be reported, then I would put it as an unrelated case, I believe, because of the history of the case. But if the diagnosis is unknown, then it would be among the unknown cases. Why the child died of such a simple surgical thing is another question. I believe it wasn't a hospital that was able to offer a high quality service to everybody because of the conditions in which the hospital operated. So I can imagine that some patients died of medical complications or whatever; right? I can't distinguish how many cases of this kind were there, but this is another issue, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on, madam, to chapter 3.4 and look at table 8. It's page 11 of the English. Table 8. Age and sex distribution of victims, men and women separately. My first question is this: In views of the laws prevailing in Bosnia and Herzegovina that recruits range from the ages of 16 to 65, why did you have the group for 15 to 19 and a group from 60 to 64 and not to 65? Why did you choose groups which do not correspond to the laws governing conscripts in case of war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these groups are the usual age groups used in demographic analysis, so this is why they were used. But, of course, any age grouping is possible, and if you want to see 16 to 65, I can provide this age distribution as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I think such a distribution would be more precise, but what is interesting here is the following: The ratio of men who were killed, according to the records of the war hospital, it says 375 males, and the ratio of males to females is 4.3 to 1; whereas, in the death registers of Mostar -- East Mostar, it's 296 men and 76 women, and the ratio is 3.821. My question is the following: At that time, in Mostar, were there 4.3 or 3.8 per cent less women, in view of the fact that women died less from shelling, which had to do with the whole town? Were there fewer women in Eastern Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you today that I didn't have population data on East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, just say, "I don't know," madam.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] So from the ratio 4.3 or 3.821, concerning the shelling of East Mostar, Their Honours can draw their own conclusion as to who was killed and how in particular places.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's go to table 9. Table 9. You say, East Mostar records in the war hospital, and this is the sex distribution. And we have the war hospital records and the death registers, and then, again, the ratio of men to women is 7 to 1. Shelling, 65 men and 45 women. The ratio is 3.6 to 1. And in the death records, it's 271 men, and accidents and woundings are very different. Is this table correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the table is correct. There are no sex ratio in the table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it can be calculated, and one can see whether I calculated it correctly, but you yourself say that both sources agree that in absolute terms men were killed more often because of violent war-related causes a bit more frequently than men. So, if this is the ratio of men to women dying of violent war-related causes, is it clear that men were killed a lot more, precisely because they participated in the combat operations which were ongoing in Mostar at the time? I will not ask you, of course, who was attacking who, because that's not your field of expertise, but does this table show correctly that the number of men far exceeds the number of women? If there were not fewer women there, then maybe more men were killed because they were engaged in carrying out wartime duties. Can you say something about that or not; if not, I will move on?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were many more killed, and you see it in the table. So why there were more men killed, well, perhaps, they were fighting more actively than women. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go to table number 10. Table 10 on page 1932 of the Croatian text, and we shall see that it is a breakdown by ethnicity. In the war hospital, according to you, there were 345 Muslims, and the records, the registries have a different number. There are 4 others, and 110 unknown. In relation to 345 Muslims, that's 2.7 to 1. That's the ratio of numbers to unknown. My question is: In your subsequent analysis, by looking at the names, you transformed all these unknowns into Muslims just by reading their names; is that correct? And, yes, just first answer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And, in the next table, you calculated that 95.3 were Muslims and 87.6 in the death records. What happened to those 110 when calculating these percentages? Do they account for 30 per cent of 345? You are saying there were 95.3 Muslims here in your calculations, but you did not take into account the 110 unknowns. This table correct? Can we consider it correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct, 110 are excluded from the calculation of percentages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And, then, in the next table, you say that the number of civilians in the war hospital was 160. There were 12 detainees, 158 military, and 142 unknown. So there were 160 civilians, and this is war hospital. Is this table correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Now, to round this off, please look at table 16. Table 16. That's 2632, page 17 in English. You say distribution of the victims of the siege according to cause of death, table 16; and then you say, shelling 76, killed 34, gunshots 18, wounding 6, and then we have unknown 404. If your table is correct, I'm a little confused by the constant changes in some information; although, for the most part, the calculations are correct, but some of the entry data -- well, is this correct that 404 are unknown? So, in the case of 404 persons, we don't know what the cause of death is; whereas, we know that 76 were killed by shelling, 34 were killed, 18 by gunshots, and so on.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is correct. But further in the text, I say that it's not fully reliable. And there are good reasons that I'm showing this table, because it's important to address problems with the sources. If I wouldn't address the problems, then you wouldn't understand what's the quality of the statistics I produced. Shall I continue explaining why the table is unreliable or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I agree that it's unreliable. I'm not saying it's reliable. I was only trying to challenge if someone says "Unknown," and those are doctors in the hospital who say that, that's the most we can have before this Court. All the rest are just statistical exercises. I can do statistical exercises myself, but here we have a fact. It's 404 unknown. This table is correct. And how we can go from there, I can't go into that. I can produce completely different statistical data. I asked you whether the table is correct, and you said "Yes, it is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like some clarification about a particular point. On this table where it is indicated "Cause of death," the first cause is shelling, and then the number of people killed, and then the gunshot wounds. I have a question about the people killed. The cause of death killed, that doesn't mean anything. When somebody's killed, there is a reason; either the person has been hit by a bullet or shrapnel, or the person has been strangled. There is a reason. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This table is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throat cut.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This table is related to merged sources, to the two sources combined together: Death registries and war hospital records. The causes are here reported according to the source, original source. It's important to understand that, in the merge, the first source from which records were accepted were the death registries; and in addition to records from the death registries, we accepted new records from the war hospital. And I explained this earlier today. This is because the personal information is much better in the death registries than in the war hospital records. This type of merge has certain consequences on the recorded cause of death and some other items, like military/civilian status and statistics obtained directly from the merge. This merge gives unreliable information about reported causes of death and reported civilian/military status. And this is related to the fact that these two items were practically not reported in the death registries, our first source taken for the merge. So this is not a good way of making an assessment of the actual cause of death distribution or the civilian/military distribution of victims reported in the merged sources. A different way must be applied in order to obtain more reliable, better statistics on that, and we did apply this other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish, and I shall give the floor to my colleagues. The Bench will have to determine the number of victims there were in Mostar, the number of people killed and the number of people wounded. If we take the lower end of the assumption, 539 people killed, and that is the lower end of the assumption due to the cross-referencing of two tables, as you've just mentioned. If, after that, I need to look into the reasons or the causes of death of these 539 people, on reading your table, 78 are reported as being casualties due to the shelling, 18 are due to gunshot; and then I have 34 - I don't know what this stands for; I have no answer to that question - unaccounted for, and then I have 404 which are also unaccounted for because the statistics are unknown. So, in statistical terms, those 34 people, shouldn't they have been added on to the 404, so as to only indicate 76 for whom you were sure, due to the cross-referencing of your sources, you knew that these people had died due to the shelling, and 18 that were killed due to gunshots. So, quite honestly, I don't have an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, killed is as reported in these registries. It is killed people. This is how it is reported, killed people. And, basically, the killed category, which is 34 persons, could be reported jointly under unknown. This is exactly the same thing. But as I said when Your Honours would make your assessment of the cause of death distribution of victims, this table shouldn't be taken into account because it is a biased table. I still do include this table to address the problems with the sources. We are not working with perfect sources. It's very difficult situation. We do what is the best in this particular situation. We have these sources, and we have no others sources. We have to live with the sources as they are. Certain things can be taken directly from the sources, but certain other things cannot. And only statistical estimates can be provided, and this is what we did for causes of death, for cause of death distribution, an estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're saying. I would like to finish off with one question, and then hand the floor over to my colleague. I understand now that these 34 people have been reported thanks to the death registries. What I don't know is whether this death registry was probably established by a municipal authority; and if I assume there is a dispute between two individuals and one dies after the fight, his name will be on the death registry, and will it say in that that the person has been killed because there was a fight or because there was shelling? This is why I have questions this. And you have taken these figures from the death registries which indicate that the people are dead. But are the death registries such that the people have been killed because of the siege, or maybe they could have been killed for another reason? Because the person who reads your table, understands that there is a connection here with the siege, and one has reason to believe that there's a direct link between these figures and the siege. But maybe there are some people who have died for totally different reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, death registries is a source established by municipal authorities. It is the responsibility of these authorities to take record of every death that occurs. These death registries are meant for all deaths: Violent deaths related to conflict, unrelated to conflict, natural causes of death. It's all there. This is the source. So, in this source, we actually, in principle, should have a very specific information about causes of death. And, normally, we do have this for Mostar. For the period of the siege of East Mostar, the reporting is extremely, extremely poor. Practically, causes of death are unavailable for the majority of these records; but, but, at the same time, when we compare this source with war hospital record, then we see there is an overlap, and considerable overlap, of these two sources of victims reported in war hospitals. We have good reasons to believe that these are really victims of the siege. So a majority of the deaths reported in the death registries for this period, for this area, will have similar causes of death. That is the rationale that we have behind taking a group of records with unknown causes from the death registries and including them, according to the criteria of relevance, time relevance and area relevance, and including these records in the statistics. But I'm not saying that we have causes of death for every single victim reported in the death registries. I can't offer this. I'm -- I would love to, because that would help to make clear decisions and produce very obvious statistics, but this is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, Witness, those 34 people who are in the registry which was established by the authorities of East Mostar, the names of these 34 people, I should be able to find them again in the war hospital registries as people having been admitted into evidence, theoretically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if not all of them, some of them certainly. The correspondence of these sources is not 1 to 1 that every single record reported in the war hospital is at the same time included in the death registries. In principle, this should be the case. This should be the case, because death registries is the source meant for all deaths in this period and in this area; but, in the conflict situation, it is not realistic to expect that sources are complete and correspond to each other. Sources are incomplete. Sources are deficient. Sources have misreporting. Sources have biases. So the best we can do, we can work with the sources as they are and understand the problems in the sources. And based on this, we try to make an informed judgement and produce statistics on the victims. This is what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I think my colleague wanted to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, a small question, and I'm not quite sure I admit to what degree it is relevant. It strikes me, as it struck Mr. Praljak, I believe, that in tables 10, 11, 16, you have quite a considerable proportion of unknown; and when you then indicate percentages, you simply strike those outs. Why? How is this justified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I exclude the unknowns from the cases of which I know causes of death, or civilian/military status, or age distribution, sex distribution, et cetera. And I consider the cases known values of certain data items as smaller samples of all cases that I have in the war hospital records. These are cases, well-defined cases. For the well-defined cases, I am allowed to calculate a certain distribution of certain categories reported; and considering these well-defined cases as smaller samples, I use the sample-based statistics and apply the sample-based statistics to the unknown and distribute the unknowns. That's the basic principle I use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to be sure that I understand correctly. You operate an extrapolation. You say, if the relationship between one category of the known and the other category of the known, it is justified to suppose that within the unknown, it is the same proportion and therefore I can exclude them. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 10 minutes left, Mr. Praljak -- or six minutes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, I would only repeat what you said. I do not have data for such-and-such reasons; but because I do not have, the data the objective picture is different. So you are saying that there is an objective picture that you can create beyond the data you have from the war hospital and the death registries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you call it an objective picture. I would call it statistically justified and, therefore, objective picture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So when you look at your statistics, His Honour Judge Trechsel asked you about extrapolation. You refer to a sample. A sample is part of larger set. When we have one set, in your science, that set is part of a larger set. And a representative sample is a sample that, with a high degree of probability, reproduces on a smaller scale what holds for the whole scope. So a representative set reflects the whole set; whereas, a sample is simply a random selection of the whole set.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, representative sample represents well the larger population it comes from. So you are right when saying this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: A representative sample when, for example, taking a poll of voters, a Gallup poll or something similar, represents on a smaller scale the whole picture. If you were to downsize Praljak and have a miniature Praljak, but he would also have a beard and a nose and so on, that would be representative; whereas, a sample is simply a random part of the whole set. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is random, then it would be very good. But I will help you with this representativeness of our samples, sir, if you want me to, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no. I'm saying this because of what you've said. You are comparing two sets. You say, "I have one sample, and I am transferring this to another sample because I assume is they are the same. They are coherent. They are identical." That is a comparison of two samples or two sets. My question is: Can two sets be compared in this way when, and only when, one proves beforehand that those two sets are highly similar to one another, that there is a high percentage of similarity between them in order to transmit a statistic from one set onto another set. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But nowhere have we seen this other set to which you are transferring your data. So did you create a set of the citizens arriving at the hospital according to all the elements I asked you about? Because that would then be a basis for comparing the two sets according to the principle that what applies in one set also applies in the other. Did you do this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't create such a template sample, say. I didn't. So I can't compare all these little samples, the unknowns with the template sample.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, these are not small samples. It's, in your words, around 35.000 people, 35 to 55.000 people, and we don't have this it fundamental sample to show similarity. Someone may have had a heart attack. People dying in conditions where there is no food, no water. We don't have that set, do we?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was thinking we are speaking of samples; that is, data from war hospital or death registries. These are samples. I wasn't thinking of the overall population on which -- on whom I don't any data at all. So any comparison with the overall population of East Mostar, during the siege in East in Mostar, is impossible. These data don't exist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct, madam. But, in you words, Dr. Rajkov says: 50 per cent were civilians, 50 per cent were soldiers. So to compare the two sets here, you had to have some statistical data on what civilians fell ill of or died of, so that you could so elegantly transfer them to the group of those killed by shelling. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I want to separate that I took Dr. Rajkov's statement and applied in this study. I didn't. I mentioned what he thinks about the distribution into civilians and soldiers. But I made my own estimates into the distribution into civilians and soldiers, and I did it with two different methods and ended, from these two methods, with similar results. And my results are, indeed, consistent with the results of Dr. Rajkov, but that is all. They are consistent, but I didn't use his estimate, in my work as such. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have to stop now. We shall resume your cross-examination on Monday at a quarter past 2.00. Between then and now, of course, you are not to discuss any of these matters with Mr. Stringer because you are under oath, and, therefore, you are a witness of the Chamber. So we will all reconvene on Monday at a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
